searchText: following up on the 1559 implementers' call - update on Etherscan's Gas Oracle API: https://twitter.com/etherscan/status/1423089947054002178 <@!420951281910284289> <@!552133098075193354> not sure if this is the right place to share, but thought it might be useful Yes, thanks for sharing!! I'll amplify on Twitter of course, this is the perfect place to share will add to the cheatsheet thanks! So this will return the priority fee when returning results to users? Users of the API - yes Fingers crossed Read about the Ropsten issue a week ago because most of the media refuses to write about it (this is something to be concerned about). Checking back a week later and still slightly disappointed with the way things are being handled. Not an ETH dev but a dev for the extended ecosystem. I know I don't have a say in any of this but just felt the need to get it out of my system. My understanding is that some stakeholders have/had reservations about London code being ready for mainnet but devs are unwilling to push back deployment because their hands are tied due to having written themselves into a corner with the difficulty bomb. I understand that the merits of keeping the difficulty bomb is a separate discussion altogether but if it was meant to force migration to 2.0, it shouldn't even be an issue for a non-merge related fork in the first place. 3554 (as 3238 back then) should have been pushed out in June regardless of 1559's delays. It shouldn't have been used to force action for non-merge updates. Postponing it by 2 years in 2019 was a step in the right direction and to be back at square one today is a tad bit disappointing. The fact that the consensus issue managed to escape detection so long into testing is definitely concerning as we don't know how many more of such edge cases are hiding in plain sight. It's not even the first time a hard fork resulted in a consensus failure (remember Berlin?) so it was really disappointing that teams weren't extra careful about the changes this time. ETH is second largest market cap with even more DeFi built over it, not some weekend project to trial balloon new experimental fee structures that might break everything. A LOT rests on the stability of the mainnet. London is not just random small bug fixes but a complete rework of core functionality. With how much 1559 was delayed and with POS supposedly to hit in 4 months, is there really a need to rework the fee structure and potentially break things? In the real world, where the directors have to answer to the investors, if something like this was discovered so close to launch the launch date would have been put on hold indefinitely and everyone would be put on double overtime to make sure there wasn't other issues. But this being an open source project, where corporate governance is non-existent, means that you can't just have people put in more effort or be accountable for any resulting errors. Something to consider is that the last two ACDs were when ETH price was at risk of breaking below 1.7k. How much of decision to push forward on the same release date was motivated by the fear of causing an uncontrolled price crash? How many people are pushing it so hard because they want prices back at 4k and do not care about sustainability of the ecosystem? Now that prices are more or less back to stable territory ~2.7k, it should have given room to push back the date for proper testing. A temporary price setback would be better than the fallout from breaking everything. If you guys were worried about the backlash, an announcement calling for feedback from the community that actually uses the ecosystem with full disclosure about hiccups would have been the right way to handle it. Not have repeated meetings among the same handful of core devs that have the same bias on the issue. ETH is already being criticised for being too centralised with governance. Eventually this will be more of a negative than a positive. Thanks for coming to my Ted Talk. > My understanding is that some stakeholders have/had reservations about London code being ready for mainnet but devs are unwilling to push back deployment because their hands are tied due to having written themselves into a corner with the difficulty bomb. We could pretty easily craft a PR that *only* pushed back the bomb. Also, the bomb is on a slow fuse, so even if the bomb "goes off", we can delay action. I personally don't think the difficulty bomb played any role in the decision to not push back London. https://twitter.com/TimBeiko/status/1414635059324198913 I think that is just because procrastination is a real thing. We wouldn't have tried so hard to target July without the bomb, and would have dragged our feet on several of the EIPs included in London. Delaying London just for the sake of delaying isn't useful. It was discussed, and no one was able to come up with a concrete plan for additional risk reduction based on the finding of the bug on Ropsten, so any delay would not have achieved a concrete goal and instead would have just been a delay "for show". It was proposed that if someone had a concrete risk reduction plan then a delay of London would be considered. And to head off the common retort, "more testing" isn't a concrete plan. 😄 A concrete plan would be describing specific tests that should be done, and why those tests need more than 2 weeks to be built/run. Even in this channel there were some devs from besu/erigon that mentioned the bomb influencing their decision on the issue There are definitely people who don't like the bomb and take every opportunity to argue against it. 🙂 During the debates about the Ropsten bug though I don't remember hearing any compelling reasons why this specific issue was significantly impacted by the bomb. Understand the lack of concrete plans making a delay meaningless but that's just the nature of open source projects. I read the discussions earlier and it seemed as though different teams were just deflecting that responsibility to others and then collectively deciding to just let it be. Perhaps some incentive should have been given. I don't agree with that assessment. I think people really did try to think about whether there was a void in testing that we could reasonably fill, but no one was able to come up with one. I believe all of the core developers care greatly about the stability of Ethereum, and while different teams have different risk profiles and aversions, I suspect that they care more about Ethereum stability than most people in the ecosystem. It will never be possible to catch 100% of bugs, you seem to be arguing to have more testing to catch more edge cases. But the effort to catch that extra 0.5% of bugs may take 100% more effort and is not always desirable. Side note : I don't think your real world example here is even close to reality. As someone who's worked on many real world projects it is always up to us the engineers to decide whether a huge delay is necessary or not. Most of the time, we will be pushed to ship things even earlier when possible as long as it runs first and solve more problems along the way. The severity of the issue will of course need to be accounted. And ETH is in real world, it is not in some fantasy land. ``` Side note : I don't think your real world example here is even close to reality. As someone who's worked on many real world projects it is always up to us the engineers to decide whether a huge delay is necessary or not. Most of the time, we will be pushed to ship things even earlier when possible as long as it runs first and solve more problems along the way. The severity of the issue will of course need to be accounted. And ETH is in real world, it is not in some fantasy land. ``` I was trying to draw attention to the fact that there is no similar governance structure in unregulated instruments like crypto. No directors' duties and therefore no recourse for negligence or breach of fiduciary duties if something breaks due to hasty commits. In this area, I believe we can agree that ETH is quite far from real world. While there aren't any people whose heads one can put on a pike if things break, all of the client developers I know of care far more about system stability than the vast majority silicon valley CTOs. ``` I believe all of the core developers care greatly about the stability of Ethereum, and while different teams have different risk profiles and aversions, I suspect that they care more about Ethereum stability than most people in the ecosystem. ``` I think that's a little dismissive of the various projects built over ETH blockchain. Billions of dollars riding on the unassailability of the EVM. The ultimate stability solution would be to never patch. We have to find a balance between making useful changes to the network and maintaining network stability. When arguing for more stability, one has to pit that against the value of changes being made. Just because there are billions of dollars on the network doesn't mean that we should stop updating. The majority of the core developers, who I still assert care greatly about Ethereum stability, agreed that launching London was the best course of action all things considered, and I don't think any of them are unaware of the amount of value flowing around Ethereum. https://i.imgur.com/d0WmNFF.png added burn/h/min <@!217710602519314433> is right But anyway, it’s too late \*fingers crossed\* Maybe we could find a less dangerous tool, if the only objective to push devs to stick to deadlines (and its objective has nothing to do with community consensus) ``` The ultimate stability solution would be to never patch. We have to find a balance between making useful changes to the network and maintaining network stability. When arguing for more stability, one has to pit that against the value of changes being made. Just because there are billions of dollars on the network doesn't mean that we should stop updating. ``` Again, like I said earlier, this isn't a small change or minor fix. With how much 1559 has been delayed, the window between London and 2.0 is so tiny that it might no longer be worth the risk of messing with the fee structure. Reminder that nobody even knows if 1559 will lower transaction fees at all or just result in a complete standstill in transactions because it's all theories mixed with hope. The original balance of pros vs cons was probably around 60 to 40. Imo, with the delays and the developments it should have pushed it over the threshold. ``` The majority of the core developers, who I still assert care greatly about Ethereum stability, agreed that launching London was the best course of action all things considered, and I don't think any of them are unaware of the amount of value flowing around Ethereum. ``` Being made aware and having any skin in the game are two different things. I reckon the percentage of holdings in ETH probably dwarfs holdings in various on chain projects if any. ``` While there aren't any people whose heads one can put on a pike if things break, all of the client developers I know of care far more about system stability than the vast majority silicon valley CTOs. ``` It's not about putting heads on a pike. It's more about being made whole when things break. Companies invested in these projects do have a responsibility for their assets. 1559 was never meant to lower transaction fees, it is meant to improve UX and eliminate the fee auction mechanism? What is the connection between London and 2.0 timing being close that fee structure is not worth to mess with? Both literally does not affect each other? Saying it is all theories mixed with hope is ironic, as if we don't work based on that, ETH would not even be conceived at all. We are at the forefront of the innovation and almost everything being done is going to be trailblazing new paths. If we are scared of that we should then adopt the stability ethos of bitcoin and barely change anything. Separate discord for gover

excerpts.author: _____josh_____
excerpts.content:
Read about the Ropsten issue a week ago because most of the media refuses to write about it (this is something to be concerned about). Checking back a week later and still slightly disappointed with the way things are being handled. Not an ETH dev but a dev for the extended ecosystem. I know I don't have a say in any of this but just felt the need to get it out of my system.

My understanding is that some stakeholders have/had reservations about London code being ready for mainnet but devs are unwilling to push back deployment because their hands are tied due to having written themselves into a corner with the difficulty bomb. I understand that the merits of keeping the difficulty bomb is a separate discussion altogether but if it was meant to force migration to 2.0, it shouldn't even be an issue for a non-merge related fork in the first place. 3554 (as 3238 back then) should have been pushed out in June regardless of 1559's delays. It shouldn't have been used to force action for non-merge updates. Postponing it by 2 years in 2019 was a step in the right direction and to be back at square one today is a tad bit disappointing.

excerpts.author: _____josh_____
excerpts.content:
The fact that the consensus issue managed to escape detection so long into testing is definitely concerning as we don't know how many more of such edge cases are hiding in plain sight. It's not even the first time a hard fork resulted in a consensus failure (remember Berlin?) so it was really disappointing that teams weren't extra careful about the changes this time.

ETH is second largest market cap with even more DeFi built over it, not some weekend project to trial balloon new experimental fee structures that might break everything. A LOT rests on the stability of the mainnet. London is not just random small bug fixes but a complete rework of core functionality. With how much 1559 was delayed and with POS supposedly to hit in 4 months, is there really a need to rework the fee structure and potentially break things?

In the real world, where the directors have to answer to the investors, if something like this was discovered so close to launch the launch date would have been put on hold indefinitely and everyone would be put on double overtime to make sure there wasn't other issues. But this being an open source project, where corporate governance is non-existent, means that you can't just have people put in more effort or be accountable for any resulting errors.

excerpts.author: _____josh_____
excerpts.content:
Something to consider is that the last two ACDs were when ETH price was at risk of breaking below 1.7k. How much of decision to push forward on the same release date was motivated by the fear of causing an uncontrolled price crash? How many people are pushing it so hard because they want prices back at 4k and do not care about sustainability of the ecosystem? Now that prices are more or less back to stable territory ~2.7k, it should have given room to push back the date for proper testing. A temporary price setback would be better than the fallout from breaking everything.

If you guys were worried about the backlash, an announcement calling for feedback from the community that actually uses the ecosystem with full disclosure about hiccups would have been the right way to handle it. Not have repeated meetings among the same handful of core devs that have the same bias on the issue. ETH is already being criticised for being too centralised with governance. Eventually this will be more of a negative than a positive.

Thanks for coming to my Ted Talk.
